exampleAnswers.title: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing an Exponential Expression

question.explanation:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

\[ \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x. \]

We need to express $\displaystyle \int 6xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

\begin{align} u=6x \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad u' = 6 \\[5pt] v'=e^{4x}\quad &\Longrightarrow\quad v=\dfrac{1}{4}e^{4x}. \end{align}

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

\begin{align} \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x&= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \int 6x\cdot e^{4x} \,\textrm{d}x &= 6x\cdot \dfrac{1}{4}e^{4x} - \int \dfrac{1}{4}e^{4x}\cdot6\,\textrm{d}x. \end{align}

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \int 6xe^{4x}\, \textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{3}{2}x e^{4x} - \dfrac{3}{2} \int e^{4x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3xe^{4x}}{2} -\dfrac{3e^{4x}}{8} + C \end{align*}

question.explanation:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

\[ \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x. \]

We need to express $\displaystyle \int (3x-4)e^{-3x} \textrm{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

\begin{align*} u=3x-4 \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad u'= 3 \\ v' = e^{-3x} \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v =-\dfrac{e^{-3x}}{3}. \end{align*}

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

\begin{align} \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x&= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \int (3x-4)\cdot e^{-3x}\,\textrm{d}x &= (3x-4)\cdot \left(-\dfrac{e^{-3x}}{3}\right) - \int \left(-\dfrac{e^{-3x}}{3}\right)\cdot 3\,\textrm{d}x. \end{align}

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \int (3x-4)e^{-3x} \,\textrm{d}x &= -\dfrac{(3x-4)e^{-3x}}{3} + \int e^{-3x}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{(3x-4)e^{-3x}}{3} -\dfrac{e^{-3x}}{3} + C\\[5pt] &=-\dfrac{(3x-3)e^{-3x}}{3} + C\\[5pt] &=(1-x)e^{-3x}+ C \end{align*}

\[ \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x. \]

We need to express $\displaystyle \int (x-2)e^{x+3}\, \textrm{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

\begin{align*} u=x - 2 \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad u' = 1 \\[3pt] v' = e^{x+3} \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = e^{x+3}. \end{align*}

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

\begin{align} \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x&= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \int (x-2)\cdot e^{x+3} \,\textrm{d}x &= (x-2)\cdot e^{x+3} - \int e^{x+3} \cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x. \end{align}

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \int (x-2)e^{x+3}\, \textrm{d}x &=(x-2)e^{x+3}- \int e^{x+3}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=(x-2)e^{x+3} -e^{x+3} + C\\[5pt] &= (x-3)e^{x+3} + C \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing a Trigonometric Expression

question.explanation:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

\[ \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x. \]

We need to express $\displaystyle \int x\csc^2x \textrm{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.$ Therefore we set

\begin{align*} u=x \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad u' = 1 \\ v' = \csc^2x \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = -\cot x. \end{align*}

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

\begin{align} \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x&= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \int x\cdot \csc^2x \,\textrm{d}x &= x\cdot (-\cot x) - \int (-\cot x) \cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = -x\cot x +\int \dfrac {\cos x}{\sin x} \, \textrm{d}x . \end{align}

Finally, we calculate the integral using the substitution $u=\sin x,$ where $\textrm{d}u = \cos x\,\textrm{d}x,$ as follows:

\[ \eqalign{ \int x\csc^2(x) \,\textrm{d}x & =- x\cot x + \int \dfrac {\cos x}{\sin x} \,\textrm{d}x \\[3pt] & = -x\cot x + \int \dfrac {1}{u} \, \textrm{d}u \\[3pt] & = -x\cot x + \ln |u| + C \\[3pt] & = -x\cot x + \ln |\sin x| + C } \]

example.title: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing a Trigonometric Expression

question.explanation:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

\[ \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x. \]

We need to express $\displaystyle \int 5x\sin(x) \textrm{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

\begin{align*} u=5x \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad u' = 5 \\[3pt] v' = \sin(x) \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = -\cos(x). \end{align*}

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

\begin{align} \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x&= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x\\[3pt] \int 5x \cdot \sin(x) \,\textrm{d}x &= 5x\cdot (-\cos(x)) - \int (-\cos(x)) \cdot 5\,\textrm{d}x. \end{align}

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

\[\begin{align*} \int 5x\sin(x) \,\textrm{d}x &= -5x\cos(x) + 5\int \cos(x) \,\textrm{d}x\\[3pt] &=-5x\cos(x) +5\sin(x) + C \end{align*}\]

We need to express $\displaystyle \int (2x+3)\sin(x) \textrm{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

\begin{align*} u=2x+3 \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad u' = 2 \\[3pt] v'= \sin(x) \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = -\cos(x). \end{align*}

question.explanation:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

\[ \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x. \]

We need to express $\displaystyle \int x\sec^2x \textrm{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.$ Therefore we set

\begin{align*} u=x \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad u' = 1 \\ v' = \sec^2x \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = \tan x. \end{align*}

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

\begin{align} \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x&= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \int x\cdot \sec^2x \,\textrm{d}x &= x\cdot \tan x - \int \tan x \cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = x\tan x - \int \dfrac {\sin x}{\cos x} \, \textrm{d}x . \end{align}

Finally, we calculate the integral using the substitution $u=\cos x,$ where $\textrm{d}u = -\sin x\,\textrm{d}x,$ as follows:

\[ \eqalign{ \int x\sec^2(x) \,\textrm{d}x & = x\tan x - \int \dfrac {\sin x}{\cos x} \,\textrm{d}x \\[3pt] & = x\tan x - \int \dfrac {1}{u} (-\textrm{d}u) \\[3pt] & = x\tan x + \int \dfrac {1}{u} \, \textrm{d}u \\[3pt] & = x\tan x + \ln |u| + C \\[3pt] & = x\tan x + \ln |\cos x| + C } \]

question.explanation:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

\[ \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x. \]

We need to express $\displaystyle \int (x+3)\cos(3x) \textrm{d}x$ as $\displaystyle \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

\begin{align*} u=x+3 \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad u' = 1 \\[3pt] v'= \cos(3x) \quad&\Longrightarrow\quad v = \dfrac{\sin(3x)}{3}. \end{align*}

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get

\begin{align} \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x&= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \int (x+3)\cdot \cos(3x) \,\textrm{d}x &= (x+3)\cdot \dfrac{\sin(3x)}{3} - \int \dfrac{\sin(3x)}{3} \cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x. \end{align}

Finally, we calculate the integral, as follows:

\begin{align*} \int (x+3)\cos(3x) \textrm{d}x &= \dfrac{(x+3)\sin(3x)}{3} -\dfrac{1}{3}\int \sin(3x)\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{(x+3)\sin(3x)}{3} +\dfrac{\cos(3x)}{9} + C \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Computing a Definite Integral Using Integration by Parts

question.explanation:
Let's use integration by parts. We set \[ \begin{array}{ccl} u=4x &\Rightarrow& u'= 4 \\[3pt] v'= e^{4x} &\Rightarrow& v = \dfrac{e^{4x}}{4}. \end{array} \]

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get \begin{align} \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x &= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \int 4x\cdot e^{4x} \,\textrm{d}x &= 4x\cdot \dfrac{e^{4x}}{4}- \int \dfrac{e^{4x}}{4} \cdot 4\,\textrm{d}x.\\[5pt] &= xe^{4x}- \int e^{4x}\,\textrm{d}x.\\[5pt] \end{align}

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

\begin{align*} \int_{0}^{1/2} 4xe^{4x}\, \textrm{d}x &= \left. xe^{4x}\right|_{0}^{1/2} - \int_{0}^{1/2} e^{4x}\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= \left. xe^{4x}\right|_{0}^{1/2} - \left. \dfrac{1}{4}e^{4x} \right|_{0}^{1/2} \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}e^{4\left({1}/{2}\right)} - 0\cdot e^{4\cdot 0} \right] - \dfrac{1}{4}\left[e^{4\left({1}/{2}\right)} - e^{4\cdot 0} \right] \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}e^2 - 0 \right] - \dfrac{1}{4}\left[e^2 - 1 \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^2}{2} - \dfrac{e^{2}}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{e^2}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4}(e^2 + 1). \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
Let's use integration by parts. We set \[ \begin{array}{ccl} u=2\pi x &\Rightarrow& u' = 2\pi \\[5pt] v' = \sin(\pi x) &\Rightarrow& v = -\dfrac{1}{\pi}\cos(\pi x). \end{array} \]

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get \begin{align} \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x & = uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \int 2\pi x \cdot \sin(\pi x) \,\textrm{d}x &= 2\pi x \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{\pi}\cos(\pi x)\right)- \int \left(-\frac{1}{\pi}\cos(\pi x)\right) \cdot 2\pi\,\textrm{d}x. \end{align}

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{1} 2\pi x\sin(\pi x)\, \textrm{d}x &= -2x \cos(\pi x) \, \Bigg|_{0}^{1} + 2\int_{0}^{1}\cos(\pi x) \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -2x \cos(\pi x) \, \Bigg|_{0}^{1} + \frac{2}{\pi}\sin(\pi x) \, \Bigg|_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= -2\left( 1\cdot \cos(\pi\cdot 1) - 0 \cdot \cos(\pi\cdot 0) \right) + \frac{2}{\pi}\left( \sin(\pi\cdot 1) - \sin(\pi\cdot 0) \right) \\[5pt] &= -2\left( -1 - 0 \right) + \frac{2}{\pi}(0 - 0) \\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{2}. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
Let's use integration by parts. We set \[ \begin{array}{ccl} u=6x &\Rightarrow& u' = 6 \\[5pt] v' = \cos(3x) &\Rightarrow& v = \dfrac{1}{3}\sin(3x). \end{array} \]

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get \begin{align} \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x & = uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \int 6x \cdot \cos(3x) \,\textrm{d}x &= 6x \cdot \frac{1}{3}\sin(3x)- \int \frac{1}{3}\sin(3x) \cdot 6\,\textrm{d}x. \end{align}

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\pi} 6x\cos(3x)\, \textrm{d}x &= 2x \sin(3x) \, \Bigg|_{0}^{\pi} - 2\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin(3x) \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= 2x \sin(3x) \, \Bigg|_{0}^{\pi} + \frac{2}{3}\cos(3x) \, \Bigg|_{0}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= 2\left( \pi\cdot \sin(3\pi) - 0 \cdot \sin(0) \right) + \frac{2}{3}\left( \cos(3\pi) - \cos(0) \right) \\[5pt] &= 2(0 - 0) + \frac{2}{3}(-1 - 1) \\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{-\frac{4}{3}}. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
Let's use integration by parts. We set

\begin{align} u = 2x \quad &\Longrightarrow \quad u' = 2\\[5pt] v' = \sin(3x) &\Longrightarrow \quad v = -\dfrac{1}{3}\cos(3x). \end{align}

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get

\begin{align} \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x &= uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \int 2x\cdot \sin(3x) \,\textrm{d}x &= -2x\cdot \dfrac{1}{3}\cos(3x)- \int \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\cos(3x)\right)\cdot2\,\textrm{d}x.\\[5pt] \end{align}

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get

\begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\pi/6} 2x\sin(3x)\, \textrm{d}x &= \left. -\dfrac{2x\cos(3x)}{3} \right|_{0}^{\pi/6} + \dfrac{2}{3}\int_{0}^{\pi/6} \cos(3x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left. -\dfrac{2x\cos(3x)}{3} \right|_{0}^{\pi/6} + \left. \dfrac{2}{9}\sin(3x) \right|_{0}^{\pi/6} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{2}{3}\left[\dfrac{\pi}{6}\cos\left(3\cdot \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) - 0 \cdot \cos(3\cdot 0) \right] \\[5pt] &\phantom{=}+ \dfrac{2}{9}\left[\sin\left(3\cdot \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) - \sin\left(3\cdot 0 \right)\right] \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{2}{3}[0-0] + \dfrac{2}{9}\left[\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - \sin(0)\right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{9}. \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
Let's use integration by parts. We set \[ \begin{array}{ccl} u=9x &\Rightarrow& u' = 9 \\[5pt] v' = e^{-3x} &\Rightarrow& v = -\dfrac{1}{3}e^{-3x}. \end{array} \]

Substituting the above into the integration by parts formula, we get \begin{align} \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x & = uv- \int vu'\,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] \int 9x \cdot e^{-3x} \,\textrm{d}x &= 9x \cdot \left(-\frac{1}{3}e^{-3x}\right)- \int \left(-\frac{1}{3}e^{-3x}\right) \cdot 9\,\textrm{d}x. \end{align}

Finally, we evaluate the integral and get \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{1} 9xe^{-3x}\, \textrm{d}x &= -3x e^{-3x} \, \Bigg|_{0}^{1} - 3\int_{0}^{1}e^{-3x} \,\textrm{d}x\\[5pt] &= -3x e^{-3x} \, \Bigg|_{0}^{1} - e^{-3x} \, \Bigg|_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= -3\left( 1\cdot e^{-3} - 0 \cdot e^{0} \right) - \left( e^{-3} - e^{0} \right) \\[5pt] &= -3e^{-3} - (e^{-3} - 1) \\[5pt] &=\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{1-4e^{-3}}. \end{align*}
